name: Treaty with the Chippewa, etc., 1829 (Treaty of Prairie du Chien)
aka: Treaty of Prairie du Chien (1829), with the United Nation of Chippewa, Ottawa and Potawatomi
nations: United Nation of Chippewa, Ottawa and Potawatomi of the Illinois, Milwaukee and Manitowoc rivers (Bodéwadmi, Odawa, Anishinaabe)
promises: $16,000 in specie every year forever, paid at Chicago, and $12,000 in goods as a present (Article II).
Fifty barrels of salt a year forever at Chicago, and a permanent blacksmith's shop at Chicago for the Indians' use (Article II).
Reserved tracts for named chiefs and grants to certain descendants (Articles III and IV).
The right to hunt on the ceded land so long as it remained the property of the United States (Article VII).

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission found that 3,528,949 acres ceded by this treaty in Royce Areas 147 and 148 (northern Illinois and southwestern Wisconsin) had a fair market value of $2,470,264.30 and that the consideration was so grossly inadequate as to make it unconscionable.

breaches.what: On remand the Commission vacated its 1965 award and awarded the Potawatomi Tribe or Nation as it existed between 1795 and 1833 $4,104,818.98: the land value of $4,480,510.26, less the $364,901.00 consideration and $10,790.28 in offsets.

breaches.what: The Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation states that the two sections this treaty reserved for Chief Shab-eh-nay at Paw Paw Grove, which the Senate kept out of the 1833 Treaty of Chicago cession, were sold by the General Land Office at public auction in 1849 without the approval of Congress, in violation of federal law, and that no later treaty or Act of Congress ever disestablished the reservation.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation, Chairman Joseph Rupnick, testimony to the House Subcommittee on Indigenous Peoples of the United States on H.R. 8380 (2022)

landTaken: 3,528,949 acres in Royce Area 147 and the part of Royce Area 148 west of the Fox River (1962 findings). The 1973 opinion gives Area 147 as 1,525,746 acres and Area 148 as 2,162,523 acres.
compensation: Consideration $364,901.00. A 1965 final award of $2,094,573.02 was vacated after the Court of Claims ruling; the final award of 25 April 1973 was $4,104,818.98.
today: In 1967 the Court of Claims held that the Commission had wrongly left the lead deposits in Area 147 out of the valuation and sent the case back (Citizen Band of Potawatomi Indians v. United States, 179 Ct. Cl. 473, 391 F.2d 614, cert. denied 1968, as recited in the Commission's 1973 opinion). The Commission held the claim arose under clause 3 of its Act (unconscionable consideration), so the award bore no interest.

nationVoice.summary: Chairman Joseph Rupnick told a House subcommittee in 2022 that Article III of this treaty reserved two sections at Paw Paw Grove for Chief Shab-eh-nay, that the 1833 Treaty of Chicago left that land in Potawatomi hands, and that the General Land Office sold it at auction in 1849, without Congress, while Shab-eh-nay was visiting relatives in Kansas.

The Band's history says the Potawatomi lived in what is now Wisconsin, southern Michigan, northern Indiana and northern Illinois, that as the frontier moved west boundary arguments and land cessions became a way of life, and that the 1833 Treaty of Chicago then set the terms for removing the Potawatomi from the Great Lakes.

openQuestions: The Court of Claims opinion (179 Ct. Cl. 473) was not opened directly; its holding is taken from the Commission's 1973 opinion. Its exact decision date was not found, so only the year is given.
Whether the perpetual $16,000 annuity and the salt were paid as promised was not traced.
No nation statement about this treaty was found.

Audit 2026-11-08: removed the statement that 'the Commission noted the annuity was paid pro rata to all Potawatomi for years after 1843'; it was not found in the 1962 opinion (OSU id 726) or the 1973 opinion (OSU id 1345). The ratification date of 30 December 1829 is confirmed by the 1962 opinion.

plain.promised: In return for land in northern Illinois and southwestern Wisconsin, the United States promised $16,000 a year forever in coin, salt every year, a blacksmith's shop at Chicago, and hunting rights on the ceded land.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1962 that the 3,528,949 acres ceded were worth $2,470,264.30 and that the payment was so grossly inadequate as to be unconscionable. The Court of Claims later held lead deposits had been left out of the value.
plain.today: In 1973 the Commission awarded the Potawatomi $4,104,818.98, after taking out the $364,901.00 paid and offsets. Whether the award, or the yearly payments promised forever, were paid has not been traced.
